claim: The canonical mechanism for multispanning membrane protein topogenesis suggests that protein topology is established during cotranslational membrane integration.
source: The canonical mechanism for multispanning membrane protein topogenesis suggests that protein topology is established during cotranslational membrane integration.
evidence: This is a statement about the existing canonical model in the field, representing established scientific understanding.

claim: The canonical mechanism is inconsistent with the behavior of EmrE, a dual-topology protein for which the mutation of positively charged loop residues, even close to the C-terminus, leads to dramatic shifts in its topology.
source: However, this mechanism is inconsistent with the behavior of EmrE, a dual-topology protein for which the mutation of positively charged loop residues, even close to the C-terminus, leads to dramatic shifts in its topology.
evidence: This claim references experimental observations about EmrE behavior that contradict the canonical model.

claim: Initially misintegrated configurations of EmrE proteins undergo post-translational annealing to reach fully integrated multispanning topologies.
source: This work reveals a mechanism for regulating membrane-protein topogenesis, in which initially misintegrated configurations of the proteins undergo post-translational annealing to reach fully integrated multispanning topologies.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the coarse-grained simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The energetic barriers associated with post-translational annealing enforce kinetic pathways that dictate the topology of the fully integrated proteins.
source: The energetic barriers associated with this post-translational annealing process enforce kinetic pathways that dictate the topology of the fully integrated proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation data showing kinetic control of topology determination.

claim: Integral membrane proteins are central to cellular functions that include signal transduction, transport across the cell membrane, and energy conversion.
source: Integral membrane proteins (IMPs) are central to cellular functions that include signal transduction, transport across the cell membrane, and energy conversion.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of membrane proteins.

claim: Membrane integration of IMPs proceeds via the Sec translocon in most cases.
source: In most cases, membrane integration proceeds via the Sec translocon, a conserved protein-conducting channel located in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane in eukaryotes or in the plasma membrane in bacteria (White and von Heijne, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: During Sec-mediated integration, the ribosome or other molecular motor docks to the cytoplasmic opening of the translocon, feeding the nascent protein into the translocon channel.
source: During this process, the ribosome or other molecular motor docks to the cytoplasmic opening of the translocon, feeding the nascent protein into the translocon channel (Shao and Hegde, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Conformational changes in the lateral gate helices of the translocon allow sufficiently hydrophobic segments of the nascent protein to integrate as transmembrane domains.
source: conformational changes in the lateral gate (LG) helices of the translocon then allow sufficiently hydrophobic segments of the nascent protein to integrate as transmembrane domains (TMD) (Hessa et al., 2005; Egea and Stroud, 2010; Zhang and Miller, 2010; Gogala et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental and computational work.

claim: The orientation of a single TMD relative to the membrane is determined by factors that include the hydrophobicity of the TMD and the charge and length of the soluble loops that flank the TMD.
source: The orientation of a single TMD relative to the membrane is determined by factors that include the hydrophobicity of the TMD and the charge and length of the soluble loops that flank the TMD (Goder and Spiess, 2001, 2003; Devaraneni et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The conventional model of multispanning IMP topogenesis assumes that a single dominant topology is established via the successive integration of TMDs that thread back-and-forth across the membrane in alternating orientations.
source: The conventional model of multispanning IMP topogenesis assumes that a single dominant topology is established via the successive integration of TMDs that thread back-and-forth across the membrane in alternating orientations (Blobel, 1980; Wessels and Spiess, 1988; Sadlish et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the established cotranslational model, supported by citations.

claim: In the cotranslational model, the dominant IMP topology is determined by the orientation of the N-terminal TMD and is primarily dictated by the features of that leading TMD.
source: In this cotranslational model, the dominant IMP topology is determined by the orientation of the N-terminal TMD and is primarily dictated by the features of that leading TMD (Hartmann et al., 1989; Borel and Simon, 1996; Dale et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim about the cotranslational model is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The cotranslational model is challenged by dual-topology proteins, which exhibit both possible orientations of the fully integrated IMP with respect to the membrane in approximately 1:1 stoichiometry.
source: However, the cotranslational model is challenged by dual-topology proteins, which exhibit both possible orientations of the fully integrated IMP with respect to the membrane in approximately 1:1 stoichiometry (Rapp et al., 2006, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental observations of dual-topology proteins.

claim: The bacterial multidrug transporter EmrE is the most thoroughly studied dual-topology protein.
source: The most thoroughly studied dual-topology protein is the bacterial multidrug transporter EmrE (Chen et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on EmrE.

claim: EmrE can be biased in favor of a single dominant topology by introducing positive charges to any of its soluble loops.
source: which can be biased in favor of a single dominant topology by introducing positive charges to any of its soluble loops (Rapp et al., 2006, 2007; Seppälä et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies on EmrE mutants.

claim: The dominant topology of each EmrE mutant retains the loop with the additional positive charges in the cytoplasm.
source: The dominant topology of each EmrE mutant retains the loop with the additional positive charges in the cytoplasm (Seppälä et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental observations.

claim: The dominant topology of EmrE mutants satisfies the 'positive-inside' rule which notes that the combined charges of the cytoplasmic loops (i.e., K+R bias) of an IMP correlates with its dominant topology.
source: apparently satisfying the empirical trend known as the 'positive-inside' rule which notes that the combined charges of the cytoplasmic loops (i.e., K+R bias) of an IMP correlates with its dominant topology (von Heijne, 1986).
evidence: This claim references an established empirical rule in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Adding charges to even C-terminal loops can influence the dominant topology of EmrE.
source: Surprisingly, adding charges to even C-terminal loops can influence the dominant topology of EmrE
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations that challenge the cotranslational model.

claim: C-terminal mutations have a long-range effect on the orientation of previously-translated TMDs.
source: suggesting that such mutations have a long-range effect on the orientation of previously-translated TMDs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation that C-terminal mutations affect topology.

claim: The finding that C-terminal mutations affect EmrE topology is inconsistent with the cotranslational model.
source: This finding is inconsistent with the cotranslational model
evidence: This is a logical inference comparing experimental observations with model predictions.

claim: The coarse-grained model enables access to a timescale of minutes while retaining sufficient chemical accuracy to capture the forces that drive membrane integration.
source: We use a coarse-grained (CG) model that enables access to a timescale of minutes while retaining sufficient chemical accuracy to capture the forces that drive membrane integration (Zhang and Miller, 2012a).
evidence: This claim describes the capabilities of the computational model used, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The distribution of topologies predicted by the simulations are in good agreement with previous experimental findings.
source: The distribution of topologies predicted by the simulations are in good agreement with previous experimental findings (Rapp et al., 2007; Seppälä et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data.

claim: TMDs in the dual-topology mutants do not completely integrate by the end of translation.
source: The simulation results show that TMDs in the dual-topology mutants do not completely integrate by the end of translation
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The slow post-translational flipping of loops across the membrane allows misintegrated TMDs to reorient and insert into the membrane.
source: instead, the slow post-translational flipping of loops across the membrane allows misintegrated TMDs to reorient and insert into the membrane.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data showing the mechanism of post-translational annealing.

claim: The fully integrated topology is determined by the position of the loop that undergoes flipping most slowly.
source: The fully integrated topology is determined by the position of the loop that undergoes flipping most slowly.
evidence: This is a key finding from the simulation analysis showing kinetic control of topology.

claim: Other examples of post-translational topological changes in diverse multispanning IMP systems suggest that this mechanism may have generality beyond EmrE.
source: Other examples of post-translational topological changes in diverse multispanning IMP systems suggest that this mechanism may have generality beyond EmrE (Lu et al., 2000; Lambert and Prange, 2001; Kanki et al., 2002; Skach, 2009; Öjemalm et al., 2012; Bowie, 2013; Virkki et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to other experimental systems showing similar behavior.

claim: Each CG bead has a diameter of σ = 0.8 nm to represent approximately three amino-acid residues.
source: Each bead has a diameter of σ = 0.8 nm to represent approximately three amino-acid residues.
evidence: This describes a specific parameter of the computational model.

claim: The bead diameter is similar to the Kuhn length of polypeptides so that the nascent protein can be treated as a freely jointed chain.
source: This bead diameter is similar to the Kuhn length of polypeptides (Staple et al., 2008) so that the nascent protein can be treated as a freely jointed chain.
evidence: This claim justifies the model parameterization based on polymer physics, supported by citation.

claim: The time-evolution of nascent protein configurations is calculated using Brownian dynamics with a 100 ns timestep.
source: The time-evolution of nascent protein configurations is calculated using Brownian dynamics with a 100 ns timestep.
evidence: This describes a specific methodological detail of the simulations.

claim: The kinetics of the lateral gate are modeled as stochastic transitions between a closed conformation and an open conformation.
source: The kinetics of the LG are modeled as stochastic transitions between a closed conformation, which prevents the nascent protein from exiting from the channel interior to the membrane, and an open conformation, which removes the barrier to membrane entry.
evidence: This describes how the lateral gate dynamics are modeled in the simulations.

claim: Two negative charges are placed on a bead at the cytosolic end of the translocon lateral gate, whereas two positive charges are placed on a bead at the periplasmic end of the translocon lateral gate.
source: Two negative charges are placed on a bead at the cytosolic end of the translocon LG, whereas two positive charges are placed on a bead at the periplasmic end of the translocon LG.
evidence: This describes specific features of the translocon model.

claim: This charge distribution reflects the position of conserved charged residues near the translocon lateral gate that have been previously shown to affect single-spanning protein topogenesis.
source: This charge distribution reflects the position of conserved charged residues (White and von Heijne, 2004) near the translocon LG that have been previously shown to affect single-spanning protein topogenesis (Goder et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim justifies the model design based on structural and functional data from prior work.

claim: The EmrE amino-acid sequence includes four hydrophobic domains and five hydrophilic loops.
source: The EmrE amino-acid sequence includes four hydrophobic domains and five hydrophilic loops, according to both the hydropathy plot and consensus topology prediction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the sequence shown in the figure.

claim: The consensus topology prediction was generated by the TOPCONS 1.0 server and agrees with previous representations of EmrE structural elements.
source: The consensus topology prediction was generated by the TOPCONS 1.0 server (Bernsel et al., 2009) and agrees with previous representations of EmrE structural elements (Seppälä et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction and comparison with prior work.

claim: In the CG model, each TMD is represented by four CG beads and each soluble loop is represented by five CG beads.
source: In the CG model, each TMD is represented by four CG beads and each soluble loop is represented by five CG beads, as seen in Figure 1A.
evidence: This describes the coarse-graining scheme used in the model, illustrated in the figure.

claim: The N-terminal TMD (TMD1) is less hydrophobic than the other three TMDs, so its beads are assigned the V bead type.
source: In the hydropathy profile, the N-terminal TMD (TMD1) is less hydrophobic than the other three TMDs, so its beads are assigned the V bead type.

claim: All other TMD beads are assigned the L bead type.
source: All other TMD beads are assigned the L bead type.
evidence: This describes the bead type assignment for TMDs 2-4.

claim: Each K bead type is assigned a +2 charge, following previous work.
source: Each K bead type is assigned a +2 charge, following previous work (Zhang and Miller, 2012a).
evidence: This describes the charge assignment in the model, based on prior work.

claim: Negative charges are excluded from the CG representation of EmrE, because EmrE exhibits a small number of such charges.
source: Negative charges are excluded from the CG representation of EmrE, because EmrE exhibits a small number of such charges (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This justifies a modeling choice based on the sequence composition.

claim: The experimentally studied EmrE mutations focus only on the addition/removal of positively charged residues.
source: and because the experimentally studied EmrE mutations focus only on the addition/removal of positively charged residues (Seppälä et al., 2010).
evidence: This justifies the modeling choice based on the experimental design.

claim: The effect of negatively charged residues in the CG simulation was explicitly tested and was found to be minor.
source: Nonetheless, the effect of negatively charged residues in the CG simulation was explicitly tested in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and was found to be minor.
evidence: This claim is supported by additional simulation data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The results of the simulations are robust with respect to changes in the modeling of TMD1 hydrophobicity.
source: Similarly, the results of the simulations are robust with respect to changes in the modeling of TMD1 hydrophobicity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by robustness tests shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The results of the simulations are robust with respect to changes in loop length.

claim: Translation is performed by adding a new CG bead to the C-terminus of the nascent protein and attaching it to the ribosome exit channel.
source: Translation is performed by adding a new CG bead to the C-terminus of the nascent protein and attaching it to the ribosome exit channel

source: The simulation is then continued for 125 ms before the next bead is added, a simulation time which corresponds to a translation rate of 24 residues/s (Bilgin et al., 1992).

claim: The ribosome remains bound to the translocon for the duration of all simulations.
source: The ribosome remains bound to the translocon for the duration of all simulations (Potter and Nicchitta, 2002; Schaltetzky and Rapoport, 2006).

claim: It is assumed that upon reaching configurations in which all of the TMDs are integrated into the membrane, the protein topology remains irreversibly fixed for all subsequent times.
source: Specifically, it is assumed that upon reaching configurations in which all of the TMDs are integrated into the membrane, the protein topology remains irreversibly fixed for all subsequent times
evidence: This describes an assumption made in the simulation protocol.

claim: Physical processes that may lead to irreversibility of topology include the dimerization of EmrE proteins to form functional channels in the membrane.
source: physical processes that may lead to this irreversibility include the dimerization of EmrE proteins to form functional channels in the membrane (Lloris-Garcerá et al., 2012)

source: or the degradation of undimerized EmrE proteins prior to topological inversion (Woodall et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on EmrE degradation.

claim: For each mutant, 250 independent trajectories are performed for a total of 4000 CG trajectories and nearly 6000 min of aggregate simulation time.
source: For each mutant, 250 independent trajectories are performed for a total of 4000 CG trajectories and nearly 6000 min of aggregate simulation time.
evidence: This describes the computational effort invested in the study.

claim: For all 16 of the EmrE and nEmrE mutants with single added charges studied by Seppälä et al. (2010), the simulations correctly predict the dominant topology for nearly all of the proteins considered.
source: It is clear from Figure 2 that the simulations are in excellent qualitative agreement with the experiments by correctly predicting the near 1:1 stoichiometry of wild-type EmrE and identifying the dominant topology for nearly all of the proteins considered.

source: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 illustrates that the distribution of topologies determined experimentally and the distribution of topologies measured from the simulations are linearly correlated (Pearson correlation coefficient, r = 0.92)

claim: All mutants, with the exception of A52K, have the same dominant topology in the simulations as in the experiments within the statistical error.
source: All mutants, with the exception of A52K, have the same dominant topology in the simulations as in the experiments within the statistical error.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation and experimental results.

claim: The agreement between simulations and experiments suggests that the CG model correctly reproduces the essential molecular features of topogenesis.
source: The agreement between simulations and experiments suggests that the CG model correctly reproduces the essential molecular features of topogenesis
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the good agreement between simulation and experiment.

claim: Over 90% of the CB mutant trajectories reach the Ncyto/Ccyto topology within 3 s following the completion of translation and thus rapidly integrate as expected for the cotranslational model.
source: Over 90% of the CB mutant trajectories reach the Ncyto/Ccyto topology within 3 s following the completion of translation and thus rapidly integrate as expected for the cotranslational model (Blobel, 1980; Wessels and Spiess, 1988; Sadlish et al., 2005)

claim: All variants of EmrE reach a fully integrated topology much more slowly than the CB mutant, requiring hundreds of seconds for some CG trajectories to fully integrate.
source: In contrast, all variants of EmrE reach a fully integrated topology much more slowly, requiring hundreds of seconds for some CG trajectories to fully integrate (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: The slow post-translational integration of the dual-topology EmrE mutants is due to the fact that a significant fraction of trajectories exhibit configurations in which some TMDs are not fully integrated at the end of translation.
source: The slow post-translational integration of the dual-topology EmrE mutants is due to the fact that a significant fraction of trajectories exhibit configurations in which some TMDs are not fully integrated at the end of translation.

claim: TMDs in the CB mutant integrate sequentially with near 100% efficiency during translation, which is consistent with the standard cotranslational model of topogenesis.
source: TMDs in the CB mutant integrate sequentially with near 100% efficiency during translation, which is consistent with the standard cotranslational model of topogenesis (c.f. Figure 1)

claim: The TMDs of EmrE exhibit only partial integration, even at long times following the completion of translation.
source: In contrast, the TMDs of EmrE exhibit only partial integration, even at long times following the completion of translation.

claim: Various experiments have indicated that configurations with misintegrated TMDs arise due to frustration from charges placed in consecutive loops.
source: Various experiments have indicated that such configurations with misintegrated TMDs arise due to frustration from charges placed in consecutive loops (Gafvelin and von Heijne, 1994)

claim: Configurations with misintegrated TMDs arise due to the strong orientational preference of a neighboring TMD.

claim: The mechanism of kinetic annealing of the end-of-translation ensemble involves two basic steps.
source: This mechanism, which we refer to as kinetic annealing of the end-of-translation (EOT) ensemble, is illustrated in Figure 4 and involves two basic steps.

claim: In the first step, the cotranslational integration (or misintegration) of each TMD leads to an ensemble of IMP configurations associated with the time at which ribosomal translation completes.
source: In the first step, the cotranslational integration (or misintegration) of each TMD leads to an ensemble of IMP configurations associated with the time at which ribosomal translation completes; we call this set of configurations the EOT ensemble.
evidence: This describes the first step of the proposed mechanism.

claim: In the second step of the proposed mechanism, configurations in the EOT ensemble anneal toward a fully integrated topology as a function of time as loops post-translationally flip across the membrane.
source: In the second step of the proposed mechanism, configurations in the EOT ensemble anneal toward a fully integrated topology as a function of time as loops post-translationally flip across the membrane.
evidence: This describes the second step of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The rate at which the soluble loops undergo post-translational flipping is a key determinant of the fully integrated topology.
source: The rate at which the soluble loops undergo post-translational flipping is a key determinant of the fully integrated topology.

claim: Electrostatic interactions between highly-charged loops and the translocon favor their cytoplasmic retention.

claim: The slowest-flipping loop determines the fully integrated topology that is most kinetically-accessible from a given configuration in the EOT ensemble, because the other loops will more rapidly flip.
source: The slowest-flipping loop thus determines the fully integrated topology that is most kinetically-accessible from a given configuration in the EOT ensemble, because the other loops will more rapidly flip.

claim: Interactions of the nascent protein with its translocon/ribosome/membrane environment lead to significant shifts in the EOT ensemble of configurations.
source: These results support the first step of the proposed mechanism and show that interactions of the nascent protein with its translocon/ribosome/membrane environment lead to significant shifts in the EOT ensemble of configurations.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent experimental work.

claim: The mechanism can explain deviations from the positive-inside rule if the position of the slowest-flipping loop in the EOT ensemble enforces a topology in which the majority of the positive charges are in periplasmic loops, as seen for the K3 mutant.
source: Furthermore, the mechanism can explain deviations from the positive-inside rule if the position of the slowest-flipping loop in the EOT ensemble enforces a topology in which the majority of the positive charges are in periplasmic loops, as seen for the K3 mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results for the K3 mutant shown in Figure 2.

claim: Changes to the ribosome or translocon that affect the EOT ensemble may lead to significant shifts in topology.
source: A simple overarching prediction of the mechanism is that changes to the ribosome or translocon that affect the EOT ensemble may lead to significant shifts in topology.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the proposed mechanism.

claim: Slowing translation has a minimal effect on the mutants studied here.
source: We find that slowing translation has a minimal effect on the mutants studied here, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 confirms this finding for other translation rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 8 and supplementary figure.

claim: Changing translation rate will not affect the final distribution of fully integrated topologies.
source: Given that these EOT loop positions are unchanged, and given that the post-translational dynamics is unaffected by the ribosomal translation rate, these results suggest that changing translation rate will not affect the final distribution of fully integrated topologies.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results showing minimal effect of translation rate.

claim: Removing either the cytoplasmic or periplasmic charge on the translocon significantly decreases the cytoplasmic retention of the slowest-flipping loops by increasing the periplasmic accessibility of highly charged loops.
source: In contrast, Figure 8 shows that removing either the cytoplasmic or periplasmic charge on the translocon significantly decreases the cytoplasmic retention of the slowest-flipping loops by increasing the periplasmic accessibility of highly charged loops.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 8.

claim: For two of the EmrE mutants, the translocon charge mutations dramatically shift the slowest-flipping loop position in the EOT ensemble from being primarily cytosolic to being primarily periplasmic, suggesting that the dominant topology for these EmrE mutants will be similarly reversed by the translocon charge mutations.
source: Most notably, it is found that for two of the EmrE mutants (indicated in dashed boxes) the translocon charge mutations dramatically shift the slowest-flipping loop position in the EOT ensemble from being primarily cytosolic to being primarily periplasmic, suggesting that the dominant topology for these EmrE mutants will be similarly reversed by the translocon charge mutations.
evidence: This is a prediction based on simulation data shown in Figure 8.

claim: These changes in IMP topology due to channel mutations are experimentally testable predictions of the proposed mechanism.
source: These changes in IMP topology due to channel mutations are experimentally testable predictions of the proposed mechanism.
evidence: This identifies the predictions as experimentally testable.

claim: The CG model lacks asymmetric features in the membrane or environment that favor either the Ncyto/Ccyto or Nperi/Cperi topology under equilibrium thermodynamic conditions.
source: A notable aspect of the CG model is the absence of asymmetric features in the membrane or environment that favor either the Ncyto/Ccyto or Nperi/Cperi topology under equilibrium thermodynamic conditions, such as the electrostatic potential across the inner membrane of E. coli or an asymmetric distribution of charged lipids (Bogdanov et al., 2008; Vitrac et al., 2013; Bogdanov et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a feature of the model and cites prior work on membrane asymmetry.

claim: In the CG model, neglecting interactions with the Sec translocon, both the Ncyto/Ccyto or Nperi/Cperi topologies are energetically equivalent and would be observed with equal probability if simulations were continued for an infinitely long time.
source: In the CG model, neglecting interactions with the Sec translocon, both the Ncyto/Ccyto or Nperi/Cperi topologies are energetically equivalent and would be observed with equal probability if simulations were continued for an infinitely long time.
evidence: This describes the thermodynamic properties of the model.

claim: The prediction of a dominant topology by the CG model arises from the initial distribution of configurations in the EOT ensemble and from the available kinetic pathways that allow the configurations in the EOT ensemble to reach fully integrated topologies.
source: The prediction of a dominant topology by the CG model arises from the initial distribution of configurations in the EOT ensemble (due to interactions of the nascent protein with the translocon complex) and from the available kinetic pathways that allow the configurations in the EOT ensemble to reach fully integrated topologies.
evidence: This explains how the model predicts topology through kinetic rather than thermodynamic control.

claim: The changes in topology predicted in Figure 8 would be unexpected from a model in which the dominant topology of an IMP is determined by thermodynamic equilibration.
source: We note that the changes in topology predicted in Figure 8 would be unexpected from a model in which the dominant topology of an IMP is determined by thermodynamic equilibration, since the equilibrium distribution of the protein topologies would be unaffected by transient interactions with the translocon or ribosome during initial membrane integration.
evidence: This distinguishes the kinetic mechanism from a thermodynamic mechanism.

claim: Direct comparison of the experimental and simulation timescales for the kinetic annealing of misintegrated TMDs is limited by both the accuracy of the CG model as well as the neglect of external chaperone proteins.
source: We further note that direct comparison of the experimental and simulation timescales for the kinetic annealing of misintegrated TMDs is limited by both the accuracy of the CG model as well as the neglect of external chaperone proteins, such as TRAP, TRAM, or other members of the Sec complex (Sommer et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2013; Aviram and Schuldiner, 2014; Jung et al., 2014), that may catalyze loop-flipping.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations of the model and cites prior work on chaperone proteins.

claim: The topological predictions of the proposed mechanism are primarily sensitive to which soluble loop flips most slowly—as opposed to the actual timescale of loop-flipping.
source: However, since the topological predictions of the proposed mechanism are primarily sensitive to which soluble loop flips most slowly—as opposed to the actual timescale of loop-flipping—we expect that the presented conclusions are relatively robust with respect to these effects.
evidence: This explains why the conclusions are robust despite model limitations.

claim: The results of Figure 8 predict that the mutation of charged residues near the cytoplasmic or periplasmic openings of the translocon channel will lead to significant shifts in the observed topology of several EmrE mutants.
source: In particular, the results of Figure 8 predict that the mutation of charged residues near the cytoplasmic or periplasmic openings of the translocon channel will lead to significant shifts in the observed topology of several EmrE mutants.
evidence: This is an experimentally testable prediction based on simulation results.

claim: Any effect of channel mutations on the fully integrated IMP topology would indicate that kinetic effects during translation influence topogenesis, as suggested by the proposed mechanism.
source: More generally, we note that any effect of channel mutations on the fully integrated IMP topology would indicate that kinetic effects during translation influence topogenesis, as suggested by the proposed mechanism.
evidence: This is a general prediction that could validate the kinetic mechanism.

claim: The introduction of IMP mutations that significantly alter the EOT ensemble with respect to the cytosolic localization of the slowest-flipping soluble loop will influence the multispanning IMP topology.
source: Additionally, we predict that the introduction of IMP mutations that significantly alter the EOT ensemble with respect to the cytosolic localization of the slowest-flipping soluble loop, either by introducing charge mutations or by changing TMD hydrophobicity, will influence the multispanning IMP topology.
evidence: This is an experimentally testable prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: For EmrE and its mutants, a significant fraction of the IMP configurations are misintegrated upon completion of ribosomal translation and undergo subsequent post-translational annealing to reach fully integrated topologies.
source: For EmrE and its mutants, we find that a significant fraction of the IMP configurations are misintegrated upon completion of ribosomal translation and undergo subsequent post-translational annealing to reach fully integrated topologies.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding from the simulations.

claim: A CB mutant exhibits an essentially fully integrated ensemble of configurations at the time that ribosomal translation completes.
source: In contrast, a CB mutant exhibits an essentially fully integrated ensemble of configurations at the time that ribosomal translation completes.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations showing cotranslational integration.

claim: For other IMPs, a combination of these behaviors may well be expected, with some fraction of the nascent protein configurations reaching fully integrated topologies at the completion of ribosomal translation and some fraction reaching misintegrated configurations that subsequently undergo post-translational annealing.
source: For other IMPs, a combination of these behaviors may well be expected (Lu et al., 2000; Lambert and Prange, 2001; Kanki et al., 2002; Skach, 2009; Öjemalm et al., 2012; Bowie, 2013; Virkki et al., 2014), with some fraction of the nascent protein configurations reaching fully integrated topologies at the completion of ribosomal translation and some fraction reaching misintegrated configurations that subsequently undergo post-translational annealing.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generality of the mechanism, supported by citations to other systems.

claim: The importance of chaperone proteins such as YidC or Sec62 that post-translationally rescue misintegrated TMDs may be connected to the necessary process of annealing initially misintegrated IMP configurations towards fully integrated topologies.
source: Indeed, the importance of chaperone proteins such as YidC or Sec62 that post-translationally rescue misintegrated TMDs (Sommer et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2013; Aviram and Schuldiner, 2014; Jung et al., 2014) may be connected to this necessary process of annealing initially misintegrated IMP configurations towards fully integrated topologies.
evidence: This is a speculation connecting the proposed mechanism to the role of chaperone proteins, supported by citations.

claim: The dominant cotranslational integration pathway for all four TMDs in both the EmrE and nEmrE mutants is the 'channel-sliding' pathway.
source: It is clear that the dominant cotranslational integration pathway for all four TMDs in both the EmrE and nEmrE mutants is the 'channel-sliding' pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 'channel-sliding' pathway was observed in the previous study of single-spanning proteins using the CG model.
source: This same pathway was also observed in the previous study of single-spanning proteins using the CG model (Zhang and Miller, 2012a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Similar configurations to the 'channel-sliding' pathway were observed in long-timescale atomistic molecular dynamics simulations of the early stages of cotranslational membrane integration.
source: and similar configurations were observed in long-timescale atomistic molecular dynamics simulations of the early stages of cotranslational membrane integration (Zhang and Miller, 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior atomistic simulations.

claim: Only a small number of CG trajectories exhibit the 'interface-sliding' pathway.
source: We find that only a small number of CG trajectories exhibit the 'interface-sliding' pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the simulation trajectories.

claim: The dominant cotranslational integration pathway is likely to depend on the IMP sequence, and the 'channel-sliding' behavior may be less dominant in other IMPs with less hydrophobic TMDs.
source: Finally, we note that the dominant cotranslational integration pathway is likely to depend on the IMP sequence, and the 'channel-sliding' behavior may be less dominant in other IMPs with less hydrophobic TMDs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generality of the observed pathway.
